items.title: Lou Marini interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 15, 2023
items.q: like I have a song that I wrote when my son was born, called “Little Louie.”

ctx.x: Well those things happen but you know like for instance one of the tunes on the album is called “Fat Man.” And it was written probably in the mid-70s. And my friend, Joe Randazzo, who was my best friend, a great bass trombone player in New York, that was a heavy cat for the first half of his life. And then he went into like Weight Watchers — or got into a program and he was slim for the rest of his life. But that tune, “Fat Man” is a slow, sort of a bluesy kind of tune. And it’s been sitting around. And then he…

“Amigion.” So I used that as a canon. And it’s fast you know. And after a shout chorus it goes into this canon where different sections of the band — and it works out great you know. So every song for me has its own harmonic ambiance that I don’t want to go outside of, and it has themes in it that I can use as harmony parts, take segments of the melody and use those segments as back-up harmony so that instead of having a stock voicing the voicing is derived from the melody itself. And so it’s a combination of…
It’s like a little bit of problem solving and do these answers, these solutions, ever come to you when you’re not really working on it?
